newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. weather calls the tune for European feeds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. weather calls the tune for European feeds.

text.p: Weather-related price swings on the Chicago soycomplex continue to be the main focus for European feed consumers who say this will limit demand here to only the most necessary trades.
Rotterdam traders said good weather prospects in the United States reinforced the view the best bet was to wait for lower prices before committing to purchases beyond September.

"The weather situation is keeping everything very quiet and if the forecasts remain favourable we'll see the bottom of the market sometime in late August," said Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.
CBOT soymeal ended broadly higher on Friday as the forecast changed from widespread, heavy rains across the major soybean producing region of central Illinois, to scattered showers.
But the market dived on Project A trading overnight, leaving physical sellers offering meal into Europe at up to five dollars easier on Monday morning.
"There is very little confidence in where the market could go from here," one trader said.
The recent heavy flooding in central Europe was also being monitored although traders said there was little impact yet.
"It's difficult to get a firm idea of any crop damage, some say it's been exaggerated but it's just too early to tell," one trader said.
Poland has estimated grain losses of up to 800,000 tonnes as a result of torrential rains in the south of the country and may have to import to make up for the shortfall.
"The grain crop will be lower but eastern Europe is a net grain exporter, so I don't see a big impact," Van Dijk said.

He said the rapeseed crop, already badly damaged by winter weather, could be cut to around 350,000 tonnes. This compares with a usual figure of around one million tonnes in a season when there is no damage.

Swine fever in the Netherlands continues to worry compounders, some of whom face demand cuts of up to a 90 percent. Traders cited the spread of the outbreak to a new area and the government's decision to cut Dutch pig numbers by 25 percent in 1998.
Van Dijk reckoned Dutch pigfeed production could fall to 5.3 million tonnes in 1998 from 7.5 million in 1996.
"No-one knows when the disease will controlled, so that demand figure could be even lower," he said.
